# Chapter 4 — Statistical Inference and Hypothesis Testing

```{r}
# PURPOSE: Create the chapter case-study dataset.
# Fix the random seed so the same simulated data appear after every Knit.
set.seed(4406)
# Choose the number of users in the subscription experiment.
n_users <- 4000
# Create the synthetic users and randomized offer groups.
stream <- data.frame(user_id=seq_len(n_users), avid=rbinom(n_users,1,.35), offer=rbinom(n_users,1,.50))
stream$watch_hours <- pmax(0,round(rnorm(n_users,6+4*stream$avid,2.5),1))
# Simulate whether each customer renews.
stream$renew <- rbinom(n_users,1,plogis(-.25+.65*stream$avid+.22*stream$offer))
# Calculate the amount of revenue generated per customer.
stream$revenue <- round(pmax(0,12 + 5*stream$renew + 1.2*stream$offer + 0.3*stream$watch_hours + rnorm(n_users,0,3)),2)
# A deliberately biased respondent survey, oversampling avid users.
stream$surveyed <- rbinom(n_users,1,ifelse(stream$avid==1,.80,.15))
# Show the first few rows to check that the table was created correctly.
head(stream,6)
```

## 4.1 What is statistical inference?

### Basic mathematical formula

$$
\widehat p=\frac{\text{renewals}}{\text{customers}}
$$

### What each symbol means

- $Y_i$ = 1 when user $i$ renews.
- $n$ = sample size.
- $\widehat p$ = estimated renewal probability.

```{r}
# PURPOSE: What is statistical inference?
# Prepare sample users for the next calculation.
sample_users <- stream[sample(nrow(stream),300),]
# Calculate the observed statistic pilot rate from the case-study data.
pilot_rate <- mean(sample_users$renew)
# Print the named results so you can compare their values.
c(pilot_rate=pilot_rate,full_dataset_rate=mean(stream$renew))
# Draw a bar chart for the calculated groups or probabilities.
```

## 4.2 Population, sample and parameters

$$
\widehat p=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}Y_i}{n}
$$

- $p$ = true population renewal share.
- $Y_i$ = indicator for user $i$.
- $\widehat p$ = sample estimate.
- $n$ = respondents.

```{r}
# PURPOSE: Population, sample and parameters.
# Fix the random seed so the same simulated data appear after every Knit.
set.seed(441)
# Prepare s for the next calculation.
s <- stream[sample(seq_len(nrow(stream)),400),]
# Print the named results so you can compare their values.
c(population_proxy=mean(stream$renew),sample_estimate=mean(s$renew),n=nrow(s))
# Make a simple graph so the numeric result is easier to understand.
```

## 4.3 Sampling bias: who answers surveys?

$$
\mathrm{Bias}(\widehat\theta)=E[\widehat\theta]-\theta
$$

- $\widehat\theta$ = estimator (mean hours).
- $\theta$ = population target.
- $E$ = average over possible repeated samples.

```{r}
# PURPOSE: Sampling bias: who answers surveys?
# Calculate the observed statistic hours compare from the case-study data.
hours_compare <- c(all_users=mean(stream$watch_hours), survey_respondents=mean(stream$watch_hours[stream$surveyed==1]))
hours_compare
# Draw a bar chart for the calculated groups or probabilities.
```

```{r}
# UNIVERSITY LAB: a survey selection mechanism can bias estimates.
# Report response rates and watch-hours across avid/non-avid groups.
with(stream, tapply(surveyed, avid, mean))
with(stream, tapply(watch_hours, surveyed, mean))
```

```{r}
barplot(hours_compare,col=c("steelblue","tomato"), ylab="Mean watch hours",main="Opt-in surveys oversample avid users")
```

## 4.4 Point estimates: difference between groups

$$
\widehat\Delta=\widehat p_1-\widehat p_0
$$

- $\widehat p_1$ = renewal rate with offer.
- $\widehat p_0$ = rate without.
- $\widehat\Delta$ = difference in **percentage points**.

```{r}
# PURPOSE: Point estimates: difference between groups.
# Calculate group-by-group averages or rates for rates.
rates <- tapply(stream$renew,stream$offer,mean)
# Prepare difference for the next calculation.
difference <- rates[2]-rates[1]
# Print the named results so you can compare their values.
c(no_offer=rates[1],offer=rates[2],absolute_difference=difference)
# Draw a bar chart for the calculated groups or probabilities.
```

```{r}
barplot(rates,names.arg=c("No offer","Offer"),ylim=c(0,.8),
        col=c("grey75","steelblue"),ylab="Renewal rate",
        main="Estimated effect of the loyalty offer")
```

## 4.5 Standard error: how noisy is the estimate?

### Math & R Code

$$
SE(\widehat\Delta)=\sqrt{\frac{\widehat p_1(1-\widehat p_1)}{n_1}+\frac{\widehat p_0(1-\widehat p_0)}{n_0}}
$$

- $n_1,n_0$ = group sizes.
- $\widehat p_1,\widehat p_0$ = renewal rates.
- $SE$ = standard error of the difference.

```{r}
# PURPOSE: Standard error: how noisy is the estimate?
# Add values or count events to obtain n0.
# Calculate the observed statistic n0 from the case-study data.
n0 <- sum(stream$offer==0); n1 <- sum(stream$offer==1)
# Take the square root to calculate se diff.
se_diff <- sqrt(rates[2]*(1-rates[2])/n1 + rates[1]*(1-rates[1])/n0)
# Print the named results so you can compare their values.
c(difference=difference,standard_error=se_diff)
# Make a simple graph so the numeric result is easier to understand.
```

```{r}
plot(c(-1,1),c(0,0),type="n",xlim=c(-.1,.1),ylim=c(0,2),yaxt="n",
     xlab="Difference in renewal rate",ylab="",main="Estimate ± two SE")
segments(difference-2*se_diff,1,difference+2*se_diff,1,lwd=5,col="steelblue")
points(difference,1,pch=19,col="tomato",cex=2)
abline(v=0,lty=2)
```

## 4.6 Confidence intervals: plausible effect sizes

$$
\mathrm{95\%\ CI}\approx\mathrm{estimate}\pm1.96\times SE
$$

- $\widehat\Delta$ = measured effect.
- $SE$ = estimated uncertainty.
- 1.96 = standard normal cutoff for an approximate 95% interval.
